What is Transformer Turns Ratio?
Transformer turns ratio is just the count of how many times the wire wraps around the primary winding compared to the secondary. This ratio sets how much the transformer changes the voltage from one side to the other—step up or step down.
Simple Explanation

Turns Ratio: V 1 /V 2 = N 1 /N 2
Current Relationship: I 1 /I 2 = N 2 /N 1 = V 2 /V 1
Power Conservation: P 1 = P 2 = V 1 × I 1 = V 2 × I 2
Where: V = Voltage, N = Number of turns, I = Current, P = Power
Simple Example
Primary voltage (V₁) = 120V, Secondary voltage (V₂) = 24V, Power = 48W Turns ratio = 120 / 24 = 5:1 Primary current = 48W / 120V = 0.4A Secondary current = 48W / 24V = 2A
Complete Technical Guide to Transformer Turns Ratio
Step-up Transformers: If you have more turns on the secondary than the primary (N₁ < N₂), the transformer increases voltage. This shows up in high-voltage transmission and special actuator setups needing higher voltage.
Step-down Transformers: Most typical setups need to reduce voltage—primary turns higher than secondary (N₁ > N₂).

Turns and turns ratio The number of turns on each coil is important; this information enables us to calculate the output or secondary voltage. If the number of turns on the primary and secondary are denoted by Np and Ns then three cases arise. (i) Ns = Np (ii) Ns > Np and (iii) Ns < Np .
(i) If Ns = Np then the alternating voltage induced in the secondary equals the alternating voltage applied to the primary. ie Vs = Vp .( this is a rare use of transformers) (ii) If Ns > Np then the alternating voltage induced in the secondary is greater than the alternating voltage applied to the primary. ie Vs > Vp .
In this case where the pd is increased, the transformer is described as being ‘step up’ (iii) If Ns < Np then the alternating voltage induced in the secondary is less than the alternating voltage applied to the primary. ie Vs < Vp . Here the voltage is reduced and the transformer is described as ‘step down’.

results.title: Transformers | Physics II
excerpts:
Taking the ratio of these last two equations yields a useful relationship:
[latex]\frac{{V}_{\text{s}}}{{V}_{\text{p}}}=\frac{{N}_{\text{s}}}{{N}_{\text{p}}}\[/latex]
This is known as the transformer equation , and it simply states that the ratio of the secondary to primary voltages in a transformer equals the ratio of the number of loops in their coils. The output voltage of a transformer can be less than, greater than, or equal to the input voltage, depending on the ratio of the number of loops in their coils.
A battery charger meant for a series connection of ten nickel-cadmium batteries (total emf of 12.5 V DC) needs to have a 15.0 V output to charge the batteries. It uses a step-down transformer with a 200-loop primary and a 120 V input. (a) How many loops should there be in the secondary coil?
transformer: a device that transforms voltages from one value to another using induction
